TBI treatment strategy and treatment effect based on DAMPs

TBI treatment strategy and treatment effect based on DAMPs. Given the connection between DAMPs and TBI, several pharmacological agents have been explored in clinical or experimental settings, resulting in DAMP-related treatment strategies. The primary mechanisms of these strategies include: reduction of DAMP production: This can be achieved by decreasing the expression of related DAMP precursors or of DAMPs themselves, utilizing agents such as apocynin and minocycline; inhibition of DAMP binding to receptors: Competitive or noncompetitive inhibitors can block downstream signaling pathways, as demonstrated by compounds such as arundic acid, papaverine, and curcumin; decreased release of DAMPs from cells: This can be accomplished by targeting the primary DAMP release pathways, such as those related to exosomes, lysosomes, necroptosis, apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and DAMP translocation, by using agents such as glycyrrhizin and ethyl pyruvate. The reported effects of these treatment strategies include: anti-neuroinflammation: This involves reducing the release of inflammatory factors, minimizing axonal damage, decreasing ROS accumulation, limiting DAMP release, and preserving synapses. Furthermore, these strategies inhibit the decline of neurotrophic factors in microglia and astrocytes, preventing their polarization toward the pro-inflammatory M1 microglial and A1 astrocyte phenotypes, respectively, while promoting an anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective M2 microglial and A2 astrocyte phenotype, respectively. For instance, glycyrrhizin administered via intravenous injection in the fluid percussion injury rat model achieved anti-neuroinflammatory effects and improved neurocognition. In a lipopolysaccharide-induced TBI mouse model, curcumin reduced the release of inflammatory mediators and inhibited neuronal apoptosis. Anti-brain edema: This entails reducing the severity of brain edema through the mitigation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and regulation of ATP and Ca2+ levels. For example, in a weight-drop mouse model, papaverine competitively binds to RAGE, resulting in reduced brain edema, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, and neuroprotection while also inhibiting upstream S100B expression. Similarly, apocynin was used to lower NOX2 expression, an enzyme responsible for ROS generation, indirectly reducing ROS levels and achieving multiple therapeutic effects, including diminished brain edema, cell apoptosis, neuronal death, and inflammatory factor release. Promoting neuronal and myelin repair and maintaining blood–brain barrier integrity: For instance, EPO has been shown to reduce neuroinflammation by activating pathways that lower ROS levels, thereby promoting neuronal regeneration and repair and mitigating microglial activation. Anti-neuronal programmed cell death: This includes inhibition of cell death mechanisms, such as apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis. For example, in the weight-drop TBI mouse model, apocynin effectively reduced NOX2 expression, indirectly lowering ROS generation and achieving therapeutic effects, such as a reduction in brain edema, cell apoptosis, neuronal death, and inflammatory factor release. DAMPs damage-associated molecular patterns, TBI traumatic brain injury, ROS reactive oxygen species, RAGE receptor of advanced glycation endproducts, S100B S100 Calcium Binding Protein B, NOX2 NADPH oxidase 2, EPO erythropoietin
